# ingestion performance


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

### What this measures

The retrieval evals measure what litesearch finds. This one measures
what it costs to put documents in: parsing, chunking, embedding, SQLite
writes, keeping the vector index up to date, and building an entity
graph. A corpus of a million documents fails on the write side long
before it fails on the read side, and the retrieval evals would never
have shown that.

Everything here runs through `evals/ingest_bench.py`, on the same
`evals.corpus` documents the retrieval evals use, split into as many
documents as a run needs.
[`hash_embed`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/utils.html#hash_embed),
a model-free hashing embedder from `litesearch.utils`, stands in for the
encoder, so the timings are litesearch’s own overhead and not model
inference. Pass `--encoder potion` to put a real model back in.

Read the exponent, not the throughput. A cost per document only means
something if it stays constant as the corpus grows. Each sweep over
corpus sizes reports the slope of log(time) against log(number of
documents): 1.0 means time grows in proportion to the corpus, and a
slope near 2.0 means doubling the corpus quadruples the time, which
never reaches a million documents on any hardware. The most important
number in this notebook is that `add_dir` went from 1.72 to 0.91.

The cells are `eval: false` because a full sweep takes tens of minutes.
The markdown under each cell records its output, measured on 4 CPUs with
SQLite in WAL mode, for versions 0.1.15 and 0.1.16.

Three things have changed since. The graph code (`build_graph`,
`resolve_entities`) moved to
[vruksha](https://github.com/vedicreader/vruksha), and the graph
benchmarks import it from there. `add_dir` now parses files on a process
pool once at least four of them are slow to parse (PDF, XML, HTML,
notebooks), which closes the open item at the end of section 4. And
`process_content(parallel=...)` no longer does anything; give the
connection a wait with `database(busy_timeout=...)` instead.

The speedups matter less than the exponents. Ingestion used to get
slower per document as the corpus grew, and now it does not.

### 1. Adding documents, at growing corpus sizes

HNSW is the graph-based index usearch uses for approximate
nearest-neighbour search over the embeddings. `add_doc` used to finish
with `rebuild_index()`, which reads every embedding in the store and
builds the whole HNSW graph again. That costs time in proportion to the
corpus for each document added, so adding a directory took time
proportional to the square of its size, all to build an index nobody
reads until ingestion is over.

`add_doc` now adds only the new document’s vectors to the index, as
`sync` always did. `add_dir` treats the whole walk as a bulk load: it
suspends the FTS triggers while it writes, and rebuilds the vector index
once at the end.

``` python
from evals.ingest_bench import bench_docs
bench_docs(sizes=(25,50,100,200,400))
```

    before (0.1.15)                          after (0.1.16)
    add_dir(25)     1.64s   65.5 ms/doc      add_dir(25)    0.80s   32.1 ms/doc
    add_dir(50)     3.31s   66.3 ms/doc      add_dir(50)    1.21s   24.1 ms/doc
    add_dir(100)    8.35s   83.5 ms/doc      add_dir(100)   2.16s   21.6 ms/doc
    add_dir(200)   29.05s  145.2 ms/doc      add_dir(200)   5.06s   25.3 ms/doc
    add_dir(400)  112.18s  267.8 ms/doc      add_dir(400)   9.21s   23.0 ms/doc
    exponent        1.72                     exponent       0.91

The cost per document used to grow fourfold between 25 and 400
documents. It is now flat.

The profile of the old 200-document run showed where the time went.
`usearch.compiled.add_many` took 17.4s of 34.7s, half the run, alongside
409,730 row fetches and 407,928 `np.frombuffer` calls, all of them
re-reading vectors that were already indexed.

``` python
# the isolating experiment: same corpus, same final index, rebuild deferred to once per batch.
# run against 0.1.15 this reports the gap the fix closed.
from evals.ingest_bench import bench_deferred_index
bench_deferred_index(sizes=(50,100,200,400))
```

On 0.1.15 the deferred rebuild was 1.35x faster at 50 documents and
7.01x faster at 400, a gap that grows with the corpus. On 0.1.16 both
arms take the fixed path, so the benchmark now measures only the cost of
the final rebuild: 0.49s of 16.0s at 400 documents.

Benchmark on an idle machine. A concurrent `nbdev-test` run, 2 workers
on 4 CPUs, was enough to turn the 50-document case into 55.9s against
3.7s, with every vector count unchanged.

### 2. Writes: one transaction, and the FTS triggers

[`process_content`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#process_content)
called `insert_all` outside any transaction, so each chunk was committed
separately and SQLite’s write-ahead log was flushed to disk each time.
Batching in one transaction already existed, but only behind
`parallel=True`, a flag that was meant to be about concurrency.
[`process_content`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#process_content)
now always writes in transactions of `chunk` rows. (Since then
`parallel` has become a no-op.)

The remaining gap between a store with full-text search and one without
comes from the triggers that update the FTS index on every row.
`bulk_load` removes those triggers for the duration of a load and then
rebuilds the FTS index once with FTS5’s `rebuild` command.

``` python
from evals.ingest_bench import bench_store, verify_bulk_load
bench_store(sizes=(2000,8000,32000))
verify_bulk_load()
```

    8,000 rows                            0.1.15    0.1.16
    no fts, autocommit                     4.56s
    no fts, one txn                        0.50s              9.1x
    fts, autocommit                        7.44s
    fts, one txn                           1.46s              5.1x
    process_content(parallel=True)         1.11s              the gain, then only behind a flag

    process_content end to end            527/s     913/s     exponent 1.04 -> 1.00

`bulk_load` is 2.05x faster and still fills the FTS index, as the same
row count and the same hits show:

    bulk_load=False  1.15s  rows=8000  fts_rows=8000  hits(vessel)=37
    bulk_load=True   0.66s  rows=8000  fts_rows=8000  hits(vessel)=37

Use it only for a load. `rebuild` reads every row in the table, so
wrapping a two-row update in `bulk_load` is slower than letting the
triggers run.

### 3. Code files

Two separate problems, each costing more than it looked.

`ast.get_source_segment` splits the entire source file into lines on
every call, and
[`pyparse`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pyparse)
called it once for each chunk it produced, so the cost grew with the
number of top-level definitions times the size of the file. Over 400
files of `transformers`, `ast._splitlines_no_ff` took 47.3s of 70.0s.
[`pyparse`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pyparse)
also walked the whole syntax tree to tag each node with its parent and
then kept the nodes whose parent was the module, which is exactly the
list `tree.body` already holds.

[`dir2chunks`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#dir2chunks)
and
[`pkg2chunks`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pkg2chunks)
also ran
[`file_parse`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#file_parse)
on a thread pool. Parsing is `ast.parse` plus a pure-Python walk and
holds Python’s global interpreter lock (GIL) throughout, so the threads
queued behind each other instead of running together.

``` python
# byte-for-byte against the implementation this replaced, over a real package
from evals.ingest_bench import verify_pyparse
verify_pyparse('litesearch')                  # or any large tree: site-packages/transformers
```

Over 2,169 files of `transformers`:

                                        old        new           chunks        mismatches
    default                          159.80s     22.36s   7.1x   14,444 both        0
    imports=True, assigns=True       281.89s     24.66s  11.4x   32,720 both        0

The new parser produced the same content and metadata for every chunk.
`nbs/02_data.ipynb` tests
[`_seg`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#_seg) against
`ast.get_source_segment` on the cases where the two ways of splitting
lines differ: a decorated function, a one-line class, a form feed, and a
non-ASCII line before the node. An earlier draft that used
`str.splitlines` had 9 mismatches for exactly that reason:
`str.splitlines` breaks lines at a form feed and `ast._splitlines_no_ff`
does not.

The pool, on the same 2,169 files:

    serial (n_workers=0)      17.67s
    threads (the old default) 24.00s      0.76x, slower than serial
    processes (new default)    7.34s      3.3x

From 190.4s on the old default to 7.34s, 26x end to end. A directory
with fewer than `MIN_PARALLEL_FILES` (64) files is parsed serially,
because below that the pool costs more to start than it saves.

### 5. Graph

The entity graph links chunks through the people, places and terms they
mention. Its builder now lives in vruksha, but these fixes were measured
here. Profiling found three problems: throughput, memory, and a loss of
recall that no timing would have shown.

Throughput. `insert_chunk` took 9.3s of a 36.1s build. `build_graph`
wrote entities, mentions and edges with `insert_all` outside any
transaction, the same commit-per-batch problem just fixed in
[`process_content`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#process_content).
One
[`write_txn`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#write_txn)
around the writes took 1,000 chunks from 21.6s to 11.5s.

Cores. With the writes fixed, extracting entities was 88% of a build
(26.6s of 30.3s). Extraction depends only on each chunk’s text, so the
build is a parallel map followed by a cheap serial merge. `n_workers=`
runs the map on processes; threads do not help, because yake and spaCy
are Python code that holds the GIL. For spaCy the builder uses spaCy’s
own `n_process`, which forks once around the loaded pipeline instead of
sending the pipeline to every task. A batch of fewer than
`MIN_PARALLEL_CHUNKS` (200) chunks runs serially.

Both pools keep chunks in order, and the merge relies on that:
`ents.setdefault` keeps the kind recorded at an entity’s first mention,
so a different order would relabel entities.

Memory. `build_graph` held every entity, mention, edge and co-occurrence
window for the whole call. A co-occurrence window is a span of text, one
per sentence, in which two entities count as appearing together. Windows
were the term that never levels off. The number of distinct entities
grows ever more slowly (Heaps’ law) and mentions can be written out as
they go, but windows keep coming at one per sentence. Peak memory grew
in a straight line with the corpus, so the machine’s memory set the
limit.

Three changes fixed it, and each was checked to produce a byte-identical
graph:

- `batch=` writes mentions out after each batch and moves windows into a
  scratch SQLite table. `_pmi_edges` already read its windows twice,
  because the cut-off for over-connected entities is only known after
  the first pass, so any object with `__len__` and a repeatable
  `__iter__` can stand in for the list.
- Pair counting moved into SQL. It was the last structure without a
  bound: the number of pairs grows with the square of the window size,
  so the counter kept growing with the corpus even after the windows
  were no longer held in memory. SQLite groups the pairs in a temporary
  B-tree on disk instead.
- `for c in L(chunks)` became a plain loop. `L()` builds a list, so a
  caller who passed a generator to keep the corpus out of memory had it
  read into a list before the first chunk was processed.

Recall. Entity resolution merges different spellings of the same entity,
and `_lexical_pairs` proposes candidate pairs from groups of names that
share a token. It skipped any group larger than `max_group`. Groups grow
with the corpus, so the skipped pairs were exactly the ones a larger
corpus added, and resolution got quietly worse the more text it saw.
Large groups are now handled in windows over the sorted names instead of
being skipped. Sorting puts variants that contain each other side by
side (“polonium” beside “polonium isotope”), which is the case the
lexical pass exists for, and the work stays proportional to the group
size times `max_group`.

``` python
from evals.ingest_bench import bench_graph, bench_lexical_recall, bench_graph_memory
bench_graph(sizes=(500,1000,2000))
bench_graph(sizes=(1000,2000), n_workers=4)      # extraction on a process pool
bench_lexical_recall(sizes=(250,500,1000,2000))   # exhaustive O(E^2) ground truth
bench_graph_memory(sizes=(2000,4000,8000))        # run per-size in its own process for a clean RSS
```

Throughput. The transaction fix and the pool are independent, and their
gains multiply:

    1,000 chunks              yake         spaCy
    before (0.1.16)         ~45 ch/s
    + write_txn              86 ch/s      21 ch/s
    + 2 workers             141 ch/s
    + 4 workers             207 ch/s      39 ch/s
                              4.6x total   1.87x from the pool

`resolve_entities` after batching its index probes:

                            before    after
    resolve n=500            3.61s    1.67s
    resolve n=1000           7.43s    3.28s
    resolve n=2000          13.26s    5.62s
    resolve exponent          1.35     1.08

Peak memory, a generator with `batch=500` against a list with no
batching, each run in its own process:

    chunks    list, no batch    generator + batch    marginal KB/chunk (batched)
      2000            113 MB               82 MB
      4000            171 MB              109 MB           13.5
      8000            281 MB              150 MB           10.3
     16000         (not run)              190 MB            5.0

The extra memory per chunk halves each time the corpus doubles. It now
follows the number of distinct entities, which levels off, rather than
the size of the corpus, which does not.

Recall of lexical blocking, against an exhaustive check of every pair
with `_lex_ok`:

    entities   truth pairs   skipping (before)   windowing (after)
       1,377         1,569              97.0%              99.8%
       3,254         3,713              94.4%              99.5%
       5,650         8,193              86.1%              98.3%
       8,487        15,004              75.9%              97.2%

At 8,487 entities the old blocking proposed only three quarters of the
valid merges, and the share was falling. Windowing examines 2.2 times as
many pairs and costs no measurable time (`resolve_entities` at n=2000
takes 5.62s against 5.65s), because `_toks` is cached and `_uf_union`
skips pairs that are already merged. It finds more merges: 6,422 against
5,896.

#### Determinism

`resolve_entities` does not give the same answer twice. Rebuilt from
scratch at n=2000, it reported `merged=5896` on one run and
`merged=5891` on the next, a difference of about 0.1%.

The batching is not the cause. usearch builds its HNSW graph on several
threads, so two builds from the same vectors give slightly different
graphs, and an approximate search over a different graph returns
slightly different neighbours. This was true before the change as well.
The check that tells the two causes apart keeps the index fixed and
varies only the probe:

``` python
from evals.ingest_bench import verify_ann_probe, verify_resolve
verify_ann_probe(n=2000)          # one fixed index, batched vs the per-entity loop
verify_resolve(sizes=(1000,2000), reps=2)   # full rebuilds: shows the ~0.1% drift
```

    == ann probe equivalence (8487 entities, fixed index, k=8) ==
      looped  x3: 67896 pairs, stable: True
      batched x3: 67896 pairs, stable: True
      identical: True   symmetric difference: 0

On the same index the two probes agree exactly and each is
deterministic. The batching is therefore equivalent, and the drift comes
from building the index. Expect it if you compare two graph builds.

`verify_resolve` reports a hash of the partition, which entities ended
up grouped together, rather than of the map from each entity to its
canonical name. `_uf_union` breaks ties by arrival order, so which
member of a group becomes canonical can change even when the groups do
not.

### Sharding, considered and set aside

Splitting the data into one database per profile was measured and does
not pay for itself.

Before the fixes it made ingestion 4.7x faster at 8 shards, but only
because each shard was smaller, which shrank the quadratic cost. The fix
alone on one database (19.8s for 400 documents) beat 8 shards without
the fix (23.8s). With ingestion linear, sharding adds about 12% and then
levels off.

Reads take a few milliseconds either way at this corpus size. Searching
16 shards takes 34.9ms against 8.0ms for one index, and going straight
to a known shard saves 6ms. Neither is a reason to restructure anything.

`bench_shards` and `bench_shard_reads` stay in `evals/ingest_bench.py`
for the one case where sharding might still help: an HNSW index too
large to keep in memory. That is a question of RAM, not speed.

### Open at a million documents

These were the open items when this was measured.

- Embedding is left out of every number here. With litesearch’s own
  overhead out of the way, the encoder is now the largest cost, and it
  is the part that wants a GPU or a process pool.
- `add_dir` parsed files one at a time. It now uses a process pool for
  slow-to-parse files.
- `build_graph` uses more cores, not more machines. At 207 chunks/s on 4
  cores, a million chunks takes about 1.3 hours. The merge is serial, so
  more cores help until it becomes the bottleneck.
- `n_workers` with a small `batch` pays the pool’s start-up cost once
  per batch: 4.87s without batching against 5.33s at `batch=500`.
- `build_graph` memory grows more slowly than the corpus but still
  grows. What remains is the entity vocabulary and the edge dict, both
  of which level off rather than stay flat. The measured slope is fine
  to a million documents; measure again before ten million.
- spaCy extracts about 1.7 times as many entities as the yake fallback
  but is slower (9.5 against 16.4 chunks/s, measured under tracemalloc).
  Which is the better trade for retrieval quality has not been measured.
